L74: > anomaly, mean: the product of the cite61†mean motion of an orbiting body and the interval of time since the body passed the cite58†pericenter . Thus, the mean cite62†anomaly is the angle from the cite58†pericenter of a hypothetical body moving with a constant angular speed that is equal to the cite61†mean motion .
L75: In realistic computations, with disturbances taken into account, the mean cite62†anomaly is equal to its initial value at an cite63†epoch plus an integral of the cite61†mean motion over the time elapsed since the cite63†epoch . (See cite64†anomaly, eccentric ; cite65†anomaly, mean at epoch ; cite60†anomaly, true .)
L76: > anomaly, mean at epoch: the value of the mean anomaly at a specific cite63†epoch , i.e., at some fiducial moment of time. It is one of the six cite66†Keplerian elements that specify an cite57†orbit . (See cite66†Keplerian elements ; cite67†orbital elements .)
L235: frame bias: the orientation of the cite115†mean equator and equinox of J2000.0 with respect to the cite119†Geocentric Celestial Reference System (GCRS) . It is defined by three small and constant angles, two of which describe the offset of the mean pole at J2000.0 and the other is the GCRS cite120†right ascension of the mean inertial cite147†equinox of J2000.0.
L236: frequency: the number of cite127†period s of a regular, cyclic phenomenon in a given measure of time, such as a second or a cite108†year . (See cite127†period ; cite92†second, Système International (SI) ; cite108†year .)
L262: Greenwich Hour Angle (GHA): angular distance on the cite113†celestial sphere measured westward along the cite135†celestial equator from the cite183†Greenwich meridian to the cite136†hour circle that passes through a celestial object or point.
L263: 
L264: Greenwich Mean Sidereal Time (GMST): the Greenwich hour angle of the mean equinox of date.
L265: 
L266: Greenwich meridian: see cite184†meridian, Greenwich .
L267: Greenwich sidereal date (GSD): the number of sidereal cite176†day s elapsed at Greenwich since the beginning of the Greenwich sidereal cite176†day that was in progress at the cite185†Julian date (JD) 0.0.
L268: 
L269: Greenwich sidereal day number: the integral part of the cite186†Greenwich sidereal date (GSD) .
L270: 
L271: Gregorian calendar: see cite163†calendar, Gregorian .
L272: height: the distance above or below a reference surface such as mean sea level on the Earth or a cite128†planet ographic reference surface on another solar system cite128†planet .
L273: 
L274: heliocentric: with reference to, or pertaining to, the center of the Sun.
L275: 
L276: heliocentric parallax: see cite56†parallax, heliocentric .
L277: 
L278: horizon: 1. A plane perpendicular to the line from an observer through the cite54†zenith . 2. The observed border between Earth and the sky.
L279: > horizon, astronomical: the plane perpendicular to the line from an observer to the cite187†astronomical zenith that passes through the point of observation.
L280: 
L281: > horizon, geocentric: the plane perpendicular to the line from an observer to the cite188†geocentric zenith that passes through the center of the Earth.
L282: 
L283: > horizon, natural: the border between the sky and the Earth as seen from an observation point.

L285: horizontal parallax: see cite189†parallax, horizontal .
L286: horizontal refraction: see cite190†refraction, horizontal .
L287: 
L288: hour angle: angular distance on the cite113†celestial sphere measured westward along the cite135†celestial equator from the cite126†meridian to the cite136†hour circle that passes through a celestial object.
L289: 
L290: hour circle: a great circle on the cite113†celestial sphere that passes through the celestial poles and is therefore perpendicular to the cite135†celestial equator .
L291: 
L292: hyperbolic orbit: see cite191†orbit, hyperbolic .
L293: IAU: see cite130†International Astronomical Union (IAU) .
L294: 
L295: illuminated extent: the illuminated area of an apparent planetary disk, expressed as a solid angle.
L296: 
L297: inclination: 1. The angle between two planes or their poles. 2. Usually, the angle between an cite57†orbit al plane and a reference plane. 3. One of the standard cite67†orbital elements that specifies the orientation of the cite57†orbit . (See cite67†orbital elements .)
L298: 
L299: instantaneous orbit: see cite192†orbit, instantaneous .
L300: intercalate: to insert an interval of time (e.g., a cite176†day or a cite193†month ) within a cite106†calendar , usually so that it is synchronized with some natural phenomenon such as the seasons or cite164†lunar phases .
L301: 
L302: intermediate place (or position): the cite72†proper place of an object expressed with respect to the true (intermediate) cite114†equator and CIO of date.
L303: International Astronomical Union (IAU): an international non-governmental organization that promotes the science of astronomy. The IAU is composed of both national and individual members. In the field of positional astronomy, the IAU, among other activities, recommends standards for data analysis and modeling, usually in the form of resolutions passed at General Assemblies held every three years.
L304: International Atomic Time (TAI): the continuous time scale resulting from analysis by the Bureau International des Poids et Mesures of atomic time standards in many countries. The fundamental unit of TAI is the cite194†SI second on the cite85†geoid , and the cite63†epoch is 1958 January 1. (See cite92†second, Système International (SI) .)
L305: International Celestial Reference Frame (ICRF): 1. A set of extragalactic objects whose adopted positions and uncertainties realize the cite195†International Celestial Reference System (ICRS) axes and give the uncertainties of those axes. 2. The name of the radio catalog whose defining sources serve as fiducial points to fix the axes of the ICRS, recommended by the cite130†International Astronomical Union (IAU) . The first such catalog was adopted for use beginning in 1997.
L306: The second catalog, termed ICRF2, was adopted for use beginning in 2010.The third catalog, termed ICRF3, was adopted for use beginning in 2019.
L307: International Celestial Reference System (ICRS): a time-independent, kinematically non-rotating cite98†barycentric reference system recommended by the cite130†International Astronomical Union (IAU) in 1997. Its axes are those of the cite196†International Celestial Reference Frame (ICRF) .
L308: 
L309: international meridian: see cite184†meridian, Greenwich .
L310: International Terrestrial Reference Frame (ITRF): a set of reference points on the surface of the Earth whose adopted positions and velocities fix the rotating axes of the cite197†International Terrestrial Reference System (ITRS) .
L311: 
L312: International Terrestrial Reference System (ITRS): a time-dependent, non-inertial reference system co-moving with the geocenter and rotating with the Earth. The ITRS is the recommended system in which to express positions on the Earth.
L313: invariable plane: the plane through the center of mass of the solar system perpendicular to the angular momentum vector of the solar system.
L314: 
L315: irradiation: an optical effect of contrast that makes bright objects viewed against a dark background appear to be larger than they really are.
L316: 
L317: Julian calendar: see cite198†calendar, Julian .
L318: Julian date (JD): the interval of time in days and fractions of a day, since 4713 B.C. January 1, Greenwich noon, Julian cite199†proleptic calendar . In precise work, the timescale, e.g., cite40†Terrestrial Time (TT) or cite41†Universal Time (UT) , should be specified.
L319: 
L320: Julian date, modified (MJD): the cite185†Julian date (JD) minus 2400000.5.
L321: 
L322: Julian day number: the integral part of the cite185†Julian date (JD) .
L323: 
L324: Julian year: see cite200†year, Julian .
L325: Keplerian elements: a certain set of six cite67†orbital elements , sometimes referred to as the Keplerian set. Historically, this set included the mean cite62†anomaly at the cite63†epoch , the orbital cite90†semi-major axis , the cite47†eccentricity and three Euler angles: the cite201†longitude of the ascending node , the cite202†inclination , and the argument of cite58†pericenter . The time of cite58†pericenter passage is often used as part of the Keplerian set instead of the mean cite62†anomaly at the cite63†epoch .
L326: Sometimes the longitude of cite58†pericenter (which is the sum of the cite201†longitude of the ascending node and the argument of cite58†pericenter ) is used instead of the argument of cite58†pericenter .
L327: Laplacian plane: 1. For planets see cite203†invariable plane . 2. For a system of satellites, the fixed plane relative to which the vector sum of the disturbing forces has no orthogonal component.
L328: 
L329: latitude, celestial: see cite156†latitude, ecliptic .
L330: 
L331: latitude, ecliptic: angular distance on the cite113†celestial sphere measured north or south of the cite76†ecliptic along the great circle passing through the poles of the cite76†ecliptic and the celestial object. Also referred to as celestial latitude.
L332: latitude, terrestrial: angular distance on the Earth measured north or south of the cite114†equator along the cite126†meridian of a geographic location.
L333: leap second: a second inserted as the 61^{st} second of a minute at announced times to keep cite204†UTC within 0^{s}. of cite132†UT1 . Generally, leap seconds are added at the end of June or December as necessary, but may be inserted at the end of any cite193†month . Although it has never been utilized, it is possible to have a negative leap second in which case the 60^{th} second of a minute would be removed.
L334: (See cite42†Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) ; cite92†second, Système International (SI) ; cite41†Universal Time (UT) .)
L335: librations: the real or apparent oscillations of a body around a reference point. When referring to the Moon, librations are variations in the orientation of the Moon's surface with respect to an observer on the Earth. Physical librations are due to variations in the orientation of the Moon's rotational axis in inertial space.
L336: The much larger optical librations are due to variations in the rate of the Moon's orbital motion, the cite205†obliquity of the Moon's cite114†equator to its orbital plane, and the diurnal changes of geometric perspective of an observer on the Earth's surface.
L337: light, deflection of: see cite84†deflection of light .
L338: 
L339: light-time: the interval of time required for light to travel from a celestial body to the Earth.
L340: 
L341: light-time displacement: the difference between the geometric and astrometric place of a solar system body. It is caused by the motion of the body during the interval it takes light to travel from the body to Earth.
L342: light-year: the distance that light traverses in a vacuum during one cite108†year . Since there are various ways to define a cite108†year , there is an ambiguity in the exact distance; the cite99†IAU recommends using the cite206†Julian year as the time basis. A light-cite108†year is approximately 9.46 × 10^{12} km, 5.88 × 10^{12} statute miles, 6.32 × 10^{4} au, and 3.07 × 10^{-1} parsecs. Often distances beyond the solar system are given in parsecs. (See cite207†parsec (pc) .)
L343: limb: the apparent edge of the Sun, Moon, or a cite128†planet or any other celestial body with a detectable disk.
L344: limb correction: generally, a small angle (positive or negative) that is added to the tabulated apparent cite94†semidiameter of a body to compensate for local topography at a specific point along the cite138†limb . Specifically for the Moon, the angle taken from the Watts lunar cite138†limb data (Watts, C. B., APAE XVII, 1963) that is used to correct the cite94†semidiameter of the Watts mean cite138†limb . The correction is a function of position along the cite138†limb and the apparent cite208†librations .
L345: The Watts mean cite138†limb is a circle whose center is offset by about 0.″6 from the direction of the Moon's center of mass and whose radius is about 0.″4 greater than the cite94†semidiameter of the Moon that is computed based on its cite99†IAU adopted radius in kilometers.
L346: local place: a topocentric place of an object expressed with respect to the cite119†Geocentric Celestial Reference System (GCRS) axes.
L347: 
L348: local sidereal time: the cite137†hour angle of the cite77†vernal equinox with respect to the local cite126†meridian .
L349: longitude of the ascending node: given an cite57†orbit and a reference plane through the primary body (or center of mass): the angle, \(\Omega\), at the primary, between a fiducial direction in the reference plane and the point at which the cite57†orbit crosses the reference plane from south to north. Equivalently, \(\Omega\) is one of the angles in the reference plane between the fiducial direction and the line of cite144†node s. It is one of the six cite66†Keplerian elements that specify an cite57†orbit .
L351: longitude, celestial: see cite129†longitude, ecliptic .
L352: 
L353: longitude, ecliptic: angular distance on the cite113†celestial sphere measured eastward along the cite76†ecliptic from the cite209†dynamical equinox to the great circle passing through the poles of the cite76†ecliptic and the celestial object. Also referred to as celestial longitude.
L354: 
L355: longitude, terrestrial: angular distance measured along the Earth's cite114†equator from the cite183†Greenwich meridian to the cite126†meridian of a geographic location.
L356: luminosity class: distinctions in intrinsic brightness among stars of the same spectral type, typically given as a Roman numeral. It denotes if a star is a supergiant (Ia or Ib), giant (II or III), subgiant (IV), or main sequence --- also called dwarf (V). Sometimes subdwarfs (VI) and white dwarfs (VII) are regarded as luminosity classes. (See cite210†spectral types or classes .)
L357: lunar phases: cyclically recurring apparent forms of the Moon. The principal phases: new moon, first quarter, full moon and last quarter are defined as the times at which the excess of the apparent cite75†ecliptic longitude of the Moon over that of the Sun is 0°, 90°, 180° and 270°, respectively. (See cite129†longitude, ecliptic .)
L358: 
L359: lunation: the cite127†period of time between two consecutive new moons.
L360: magnitude of a lunar eclipse: the fraction of the lunar diameter obscured by the shadow of the Earth at the greatest cite211†phase of a lunar eclipse, measured along the common diameter. (See cite212†eclipse, lunar .)
L361: 
L362: magnitude of a solar eclipse: the fraction of the solar diameter obscured by the Moon at the greatest cite211†phase of a solar eclipse, measured along the common diameter. (See cite152†eclipse, solar .)
L363: magnitude, stellar: a measure on a logarithmic scale of the brightness of a celestial object. Since brightness varies with wavelength, often a wavelength band is specified. A factor of 100 in brightness is equivalent to a change of 5 in stellar magnitude, and brighter sources have lower magnitudes. For example, the bright star Sirius has a visual-band magnitude of -1.46 whereas the faintest stars detectable with an unaided eye under ideal conditions have visual-band magnitudes of about 6.0.
L364: mean distance: an average distance between the primary and the secondary gravitating body. The meaning of the mean distance depends upon the chosen method of averaging (i.e., averaging over the time, or over the true anomaly, or the mean anomaly. It is also important what power of the distance is subject to averaging.) In this volume the mean distance is defined as the inverse of the time-averaged reciprocal distance: \((\int r^{-1}\, \rm{d}t)^{-1}\).
L366: mean elements: average values of the cite67†orbital elements over some section of the cite57†orbit or over some interval of time. They are interpreted as the cite213†elements of some reference (mean) cite57†orbit that approximates the actual one and, thus, may serve as the basis for calculating cite57†orbit cite89†perturbations . The values of mean cite213†elements depend upon the chosen method of averaging and upon the length of time over which the averaging is made.
L367: mean equator and equinox: the celestial coordinate system defined by the orientation of the Earth's cite114†equator ial plane on some specified date together with the direction of the cite209†dynamical equinox on that date, neglecting cite122†nutation . Thus, the mean cite114†equator and cite147†equinox moves in response only to cite121†precession .
L368: Positions in a star catalog have traditionally been referred to a catalog cite114†equator and cite147†equinox that approximate the mean cite114†equator and cite147†equinox of a cite214†standard epoch . (See cite146†catalog equinox ; cite116†true equator and equinox .)
L369: mean motion: defined for bound orbits only. 1. The rate of change of the mean anomaly. 2. The value \(\sqrt{Gm/a^3}\), where \(G\) is Newton's gravitational constant, \(m\) is the sum of the masses of the primary and secondary bodies, and \(a\) is the orbital cite90†semi-major axis of the relative orbit. For unperturbed elliptic or circular orbits, these definitions are equivalent; the mean motion is related to the cite127†period through \(nT=2\pi\) where \(n\) is the mean motion and \(T\) is the cite127†period .
L372: Conceptually, the coordinates represent the direction of the object as it would hypothetically be observed from the solar system cite97†barycenter at the specified date, with respect to a fixed coordinate system (e.g., the axes of the cite196†International Celestial Reference Frame (ICRF) ), if the masses of the Sun and other solar system bodies were negligible.
L376: > meridian, central (planetary): half of the great circle passing through the cite128†planet 's poles and through the sub-earth point). This is the same as the longitude of the sub-earth point. Do not confuse with cite128†planet ary cite216†prime meridian . See diagram on page E4.
L377: > meridian, ephemeris: a fictitious cite126†meridian that rotates independently of the Earth at the uniform rate implicitly defined by cite40†Terrestrial Time (TT) . The cite81†ephemeris cite126†meridian is 1.002 738 \(\Delta {\rm T}\) east of the cite183†Greenwich meridian , where \(\Delta {\rm T} = {\rm TT} - {\rm UT1}\).
L378: > meridian, Greenwich: (also called international or cite216†prime meridian ) is a generic reference to one of several origins of the Earth's longitude coordinate (zero-longitude). In The Astronomical Almanac, it is the plane defining the astronomical zero cite126†meridian ; it contains the geocenter, the Celestial Intermediate Pole and the Terrestrial Intermediate Origin.
L379: Other definitions are: the x-z plane of the cite197†International Terrestrial Reference System (ITRS) ; the zero-longitude cite126†meridian of the World Geodetic System 1984 (WGS-84); and the cite126†meridian that passes through the cite134†transit circle at the Royal Observatory, Greenwich. Note that the latter cite126†meridian is about 100 m west of the others.
L380: > meridian, international: see cite184†meridian, Greenwich .
L381: 
L382: > meridian, prime: on Earth, same as cite183†Greenwich meridian . On other solar system objects, the zero-longitude cite126†meridian , typically defined via international convention by an observable surface feature or cite160†rotational elements .
L383: minor planet: a loosely defined term generally meaning a small solar system body that is cite57†orbit ing the Sun, does not show a comet-like appearance, and is not massive enough to be a cite79†dwarf planet . The term is often used interchangeably with ''asteroid'', although there is no implicit constraint that a minor cite128†planet be interior to Jupiter's cite57†orbit .
L384: month: a calendrical unit that approximates the cite127†period of revolution of the Moon. Also, the cite127†period of time between the same dates in successive cite106†calendar months.
L385: 
L386: > month, sidereal: the cite127†period of revolution of the Moon about the Earth (or Earth-Moon cite97†barycenter ) in a fixed reference frame. It is the mean cite127†period of revolution with respect to the background stars. The mean length of the sidereal cite193†month is approximately 27.322 days.
L387: > month, synodic: the cite127†period between successive new moons (as seen from the geocenter). The mean length of the synodic cite193†month is approximately 29.531 days.
L388: moonrise, moonset: the times at which the apparent upper cite138†limb of the Moon is on the astronomical horizon. In The Astronomical Almanac, they are computed as the times when the true cite55†zenith distance , referred to the center of the Earth, of the central point of the Moon's disk is 90° 34′ \(+ s - \pi\), where \(s\) is the Moon's cite94†semidiameter , \(\pi\) is the cite217†horizontal parallax , and 34′ is the adopted value of cite218†horizontal refraction .
L389: nadir: the point on the cite113†celestial sphere diametrically opposite to the cite54†zenith .
L390: 
L391: Near Earth Object (NEO): any cite78†small solar system body , including comets, whose orbit brings it near the Earth. A cite78†small solar system body is conventionally considered an NEO if its cite48†perihelion is less than 1.3 au.
L392: node: either of the points on the cite113†celestial sphere at which the plane of an cite57†orbit intersects a reference plane. The position of one of the nodes (the cite201†longitude of the ascending node ) is traditionally used as one of the standard cite67†orbital elements .
L393: nutation: oscillations in the motion of the rotation pole of a freely rotating body that is undergoing torque from external gravitational forces. Nutation of the Earth's pole is specified in terms of components in cite205†obliquity and longitude.

L559: week: an arbitrary cite127†period of days, usually seven days; approximately equal to the number of days counted between the four principal phases of the Moon. (See cite164†lunar phases .)

L562: year: a cite127†period of time based on the revolution of the Earth around the Sun, or the cite127†period of the Sun's apparent motion around the cite113†celestial sphere . The length of a given year depends on the choice of the reference point used to measure this motion.

L571: > year, sidereal: the cite127†period of revolution of the Earth around the Sun in a fixed reference frame.
